gloss: deal out to, do (good or evil) to; wean; ripen; a dealing, recompense; camel
summary: The verb is to deal out to someone, to do good or evil to him: “you dealt good to me, and I dealt evil to you” (1Sa 24:18). Said of Yahweh it is his dealing with a man according to his righteousness or, in mercy, not according to his sins (Psa 18:21; 103:10). It is also to wean a child (1Sa 1:23–24) and, of fruit, to ripen (Num 17:23), uses whose tie to “deal out” is not fixed by any verse. גְּמוּל is the dealing itself, which comes back on the doer’s head as his recompense (Oba 1:15; Psa 28:4), and Akkadian gimillu, “a favour; requital, vengeance”, has the same two sides. גָּמָל, the camel, is the same spelling in Hebrew, Akkadian, Aramaic, Arabic and South Arabian, but nothing yet shows how it belongs to the verb.

words.summary: The camel, a beast of wealth, burden and riding for the patriarchs and the peoples of the east and the desert, and unclean for food. The word is the same across the Semitic languages; how it is tied to the verb’s “deal out, wean, ripen” is not known, and no verse links them.

senses.definition: The camel, which chews the cud but does not divide the hoof, and so is unclean to Israel; counted among a man’s flocks and herds as wealth, and used to carry loads and riders over long desert journeys.

evidence.note: “The גָּמָל, for it chews the cud but does not divide the hoof; it is unclean to you.”
The same law: the camel, the hare and the rock badger.

senses.definition: Camels counted with sheep, cattle, donkeys and servants as the measure of a man’s possessions, and taken as spoil in war.

evidence.note: Pharaoh gives Abram sheep, oxen, donkeys, servants “and camels”.
Jacob grows very rich: flocks, servants, “camels and donkeys”.
Job’s substance: seven thousand sheep, three thousand גְּמַלִּים.
Restored double: six thousand camels.
Amalek is to be destroyed “from camel to donkey”.
Fifty thousand camels taken from the Hagrites.
Over David’s camels, Obil the Ishmaelite.
The returning exiles’ 435 camels.

senses.definition: Camels loaded with goods and ridden on long journeys: the caravans of Ishmaelites and of Sheba, the hosts of Midian and the east, and the rider of a camel in Isaiah’s watchman’s vision.

evidence.note: Abraham’s servant takes ten camels, with every good thing of his master in his hand, to Aram.
Rebekah and her maids “rode upon the camels”.
She alights from the camel when she sees Isaac.
Rachel hides the teraphim in the כַּר הַגָּמָל, the camel’s saddle, and sits on them.
Ishmaelites from Gilead, “their camels carrying spices, balm and myrrh” to Egypt.
The queen of Sheba’s camels carrying spices, gold and precious stones.
Midian, Amalek and the sons of the east: “their camels without number, as the sand of the sea”.
The watchman sees “a rider of a donkey, a rider of a camel”.
Judah’s envoys carry their treasures “on the hump (דַּבֶּשֶׁת) of camels” to Egypt.
“A multitude of camels shall cover you, the young camels (בִּכְרֵי) of Midian and Ephah; all from Sheba shall come, they shall bring gold and frankincense.”
John wore clothing of camel’s hair.
“It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”
“Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel.”
“Camel”; in the LXX for גָּמָל. The Greek word has the Semitic consonants g-m-l, as Akkadian gammalu, Aramaic gamlā and Arabic jamal do.

evidence.locator: Gen.12.16, גְמַלִּֽים → κάμηλοι; Gen.24.10, גְמַלִּ֜ים → καμήλους; κάμηλος renders גָּמָל throughout

evidence.note: “Hebr. גָּמָל”: the Greek word taken from the Hebrew.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܓܡܠܐ (gamlā), wherever the Greek has κάμηλος.

senses.definition: The camel, in John’s clothing and in the Lord’s sayings on the rich man and on the scribes and Pharisees.

evidence.note: It is easier for a גַּמְלָא to enter the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.
John’s clothing of camel’s hair.
Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel.

words.gloss: deal out to, do (good or evil) to; wean; ripen
words.summary: To deal out to someone, to do to him good or evil; with עַל, often of Yahweh dealing bountifully with his servant. Its other uses are to wean a child and, of a plant, to ripen fruit. A common thought of bringing a thing to its full measure has been proposed for all three, but no verse states it, and the cognates found so far (Akkadian gamālu “do a favour, spare”, Aramaic גְּמַל “do one good or evil”) share only the first.

stems.gloss: deal out to, do to; deal bountifully with; wean; ripen

senses.gloss: deal out to, do (good or evil) to
senses.definition: To do something to someone, good or evil, as one’s dealing with him; the thing done is its object, the person the second object or with עַל. It does not of itself mean repaying: the dealing may be the first act, and only the context and כְּ “according to” make it a return.

evidence.note: Saul to David: “You have dealt (גְּמַלְתַּנִי) good to me, and I have dealt (גְּמַלְתִּיךָ) evil to you.” The same verb for good and evil, and for the first act as well as the answer.
The capable wife: “She deals him good and not evil all the days of her life.”
Joseph’s brothers fear he will repay “all the evil which we dealt (גָּמַלְנוּ) to him”: the brothers’ own first act.
“Forgive … for they dealt evil to you.”
Do not strive with a man without cause, “if he has dealt you no evil”.
“If I have dealt evil to him who was at peace with me.”
“Woe to their soul, for they have dealt evil to themselves.”
“Do you deal thus with Yahweh, foolish people and unwise? Is he not your father?”
To Babylon: happy he who repays (יְשַׁלֶּם) you “your dealing (גְּמוּלֵךְ) which you dealt (גָּמַלְתְּ) to us”.
To Tyre, Sidon and Philistia: “If you are dealing (גֹּמְלִים) with me, swiftly I will return your dealing on your head.”
Ammon, Moab and Seir “dealing with us” by coming to drive Israel out of its inheritance.
“The man of kindness deals well with (גֹּמֵל) his own soul, but the cruel troubles his own flesh.”

senses.definition: Of Yahweh with עַל or a direct object: to deal well with his servant, out of his covenant faithfulness and compassion; and, with כְּ, to deal with a man according to his righteousness, or in mercy not according to his sins.

evidence.note: “The kindnesses of Yahweh … according to all that Yahweh has dealt to us, the great goodness to the house of Israel which he has dealt them according to his compassions and the greatness of his kindnesses (חֲסָדָיו).”
“I trust in your kindness … I will sing to Yahweh, for he has dealt bountifully with me (גָמַל עָלָי).”
“Return to your rest, my soul, for Yahweh has dealt bountifully with you.”
“Deal bountifully with your servant, that I may live and keep your word.”
“The righteous will surround me, for you will deal bountifully with me.”
“Yahweh dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he returned (יָשִׁיב) to me.”
The same song in Samuel.
“He has not done (עָשָׂה) to us according to our sins, nor dealt (גָמַל) with us according to our iniquities”: the two verbs in parallel.
Barzillai: “Why should the king deal me this dealing (יִגְמְלֵנִי … הַגְּמוּלָה)?” Of a king’s reward.

senses.definition: To wean a child, bringing its nursing at the breast to an end; the passive participle גָּמוּל is a weaned child, set against the יוֹנֵק, the one still nursing.

evidence.note: “The woman stayed and nursed (וַתֵּינֶק) her son until she weaned him (גָּמְלָהּ).”
When she had weaned him she brought him to Yahweh’s house at Shiloh.
Tahpenes weaned Genubath in Pharaoh’s house.
Gomer weaned Lo-ruhamah and conceived a son.
“Whom will he teach knowledge? Those weaned (גְּמוּלֵי) from milk, taken from the breasts.”
“The nursing child (יוֹנֵק) shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child (גָּמוּל) shall put his hand on the viper’s den.”
“I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me”: content, no longer crying for the breast.

senses.definition: Of a plant or its fruit: to come to ripeness, or to bring fruit to ripeness.

evidence.note: Aaron’s rod “had budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, וַיִּגְמֹל שְׁקֵדִים, and ripened almonds”: the last of four stages of growth in one night.
“When the blossom is over and the sour grape (בֹסֶר) is ripening (גֹּמֵל)”, before the harvest.

senses.definition: Of a child: to be weaned, the end of nursing marked in Isaac’s case by a feast and in Samuel’s by his being brought to Yahweh.

evidence.note: “The child grew and was weaned (וַיִּגָּמַל), and Abraham made a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned (הִגָּמֵל).”
Hannah: “Until the child is weaned; then I will bring him.”
“You will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.”
“It is righteous with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you.”

evidence.locator: 1Sa.24.18, גְּמַלְתַּ֣ → ἀνταπέδωκάς, גְּמַלְתִּ֥י → ἀνταπέδωκά; Psa.7.5; Psa.103.10; Psa.137.8; Psa.142.8; Deu.32.6; 2Sa.19.37

parallels.note: Yahweh dealt with me according to my righteousness, “he returned to me” according to my clean hands.
The nursing child beside the weaned; she nursed him until she weaned him.

opposites.note: The verb takes good and evil alike as its object, set against each other.

words.gloss: a dealing, what one has done; recompense
words.summary: What a man has dealt out, the work of his hands, good or evil; and that same dealing returned on his own head as his recompense. The returning is said by the verb with it (הֵשִׁיב, שִׁלֵּם), so the noun is the deed and the requital at once: what you dealt is what you receive.

senses.gloss: a dealing, what one has done; a benefit
senses.definition: What someone has done to another, the dealing of his hands; of Yahweh, the good he has dealt, his benefits.

evidence.note: “If you have done to him according to the dealing (כִּגְמוּל) of his hands”: Gideon’s deeds for Israel.
“Bless Yahweh, my soul, and forget not all his dealings (גְּמוּלָיו)”, which the next verses list: he forgives, heals, redeems, crowns.
“Hezekiah did not return according to the dealing done to him (כִגְמֻל עָלָיו), for his heart was lifted up.”
“He who is gracious to the poor lends to Yahweh, and his dealing (גְּמֻלוֹ) he will repay to him.”

senses.definition: A man’s dealing returned upon him: with הֵשִׁיב “return” or שִׁלֵּם “repay”, the recompense Yahweh brings on the wicked and on the nations, set beside vengeance and wrath.

evidence.note: “As you have done, it shall be done to you; your dealing (גְּמֻלְךָ) shall return on your own head.”
“Give them according to their work … according to the work of their hands; return to them their dealing (גְּמוּלָם).”
“Woe to the wicked … for the dealing of his hands shall be done to him.”
“The dealing of a man’s hands will return to him”, beside being filled with good from the fruit of his mouth.
“Return to them a recompense, Yahweh, according to the work of their hands.”
“Rise up, judge of the earth; return a recompense to the proud.”
“I will return your dealing on your head.”
“Happy he who repays you your dealing which you dealt to us.”
“Behold your God will come with vengeance (נָקָם), the recompense of God; he will come and save you.”
“Wrath to his adversaries, recompense to his enemies; to the coastlands he will repay recompense.”
“The voice of Yahweh, repaying recompense to his enemies.”
“Flee from the midst of Babylon … for it is the time of Yahweh’s vengeance; he is repaying her a recompense.”
“Lest they also invite you again and a repayment be made to you.”

evidence.locator: Lam.3.64, גְּמ֛וּל → ἀνταπόδομα; Jer.51.6; Jol.4.4; Jol.4.7; Pro.12.14; 2Ch.32.25

evidence.note: “From the Lord you will receive the recompense of the inheritance.”

parallels.note: Vengeance beside the recompense of God.
Their work, the work of their hands, beside their dealing.
Wrath to his adversaries beside recompense to his enemies.

words.summary: The feminine of גְּמוּל, with the same two sides: a reward dealt, and in the plural the recompenses Yahweh repays.

senses.definition: A dealing bestowed, as a king’s reward; in the plural, the recompenses of the God who repays.

evidence.note: “Why should the king deal me this dealing (הַגְּמוּלָה הַזֹּאת)?” Barzillai declines David’s reward.
On Babylon: “For Yahweh is a God of recompenses (אֵל גְּמֻלוֹת); he will surely repay.”
“According to their dealings (גְּמֻלוֹת), so will he repay.”

words.summary: Once only, in the plural with the Aramaic-looking suffix ־וֹהִי: Yahweh’s benefits dealt to the psalmist. A single use, so its sense rests on that verse and on its sibling גְּמוּל in Psa 103:2.

senses.definition: A good thing dealt to someone, which calls for a return.

evidence.note: “What shall I return (אָשִׁיב) to Yahweh for all his benefits (תַּגְמוּלוֹהִי) to me?”, after “Yahweh has dealt bountifully with you” (Psa 116:7).

cognates.gloss: do a favour; spare, save (a life); come to an agreement
cognates.note: Neo-Assyrian and Babylonian, with the participle gāmilu “merciful, one who spares, saviour”. It answers to the Hebrew verb’s dealing well, especially Yahweh’s dealing bountifully with his servant (Psa 13:6; 116:7). The Proto-Semitic root list files it under *gmr “spare” rather than *gml, so its tie may be to Hebrew גמר instead.

evidence.locator: armep x000009200, gamālu [do a favour] V
armep x000091220, gāmilu [merciful] AJ; armep x000091210, gāmilu [one who does a favour] N
SEM000996 gmr [spare] V, AKK002749 gamālu [do a favour] V

cognates.gloss: a favour, friendly deed; requital, reward, revenge
cognates.note: A deed done to someone and that deed returned, for good (favour, reward) or ill (revenge, vengeance): the same two sides as גְּמוּל, “a dealing” and “recompense”. Common from Old Babylonian onward.

evidence.locator: armep x000009270, gimillu [requital] N (meanings: favour, friendly deed, requital, reward, revenge, vengeance)

cognates.gloss: do (good or evil) to someone; show kindness
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targum of 1Sa 24:18 for the Hebrew verb, and in the phrase גְּמַל חֶסֶד “show kindness”: dealing, good or evil, as in Hebrew.

evidence.note: Targ. 1Sa 24:18; Y. Ḥag. II, 77d.

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targum of Psa 116:12 for תַּגְמוּל.

cognates.gloss: make a benefit good and liberal, act well; a good deed, comely behaviour
cognates.note: Form IV of the root of “beauty” (جَمَال): ʾajmala aṣ-ṣanīʿa “he made the benefit good and liberal” to someone, and ʿāmalahu bi-l-jamīl “he treated him with comely behaviour”. Close to the Hebrew verb’s dealing well, but Arabic gives it from “beautiful”, which Hebrew does not have, so it is recorded as possible. The same Arabic root also has jamala and ʾajmala “collect; sum up a reckoning”, which some take to be the “bring to full measure” behind weaning and ripening; no Hebrew verse shows that sense.

evidence.note: He collected; summed up; he made the benefit good and large; he acted with goodness.
Beautiful, good in action; عَامَلَهُ بِالجَمِيلِ, he treated him with comely behaviour.

cognates.note: Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian, common in the royal inscriptions’ tribute and spoil lists of the Arabs.

evidence.locator: SEM000082 gml [camel] N, AKK002767 gammalu [camel] N

cognates.note: Properly the full-grown male, the mate of the nāqa, but used of the camel generally; jammāl is a camel-owner or driver.
Jewish Aramaic, in the Targums for Hebrew גָּמָל (Targ. Lev 11:4; Gen 24:10); Syriac gamlā in the Peshitta is the same word.
Sabaean inscriptions: rkbm w-gmlm “riding camels and transport camels”; gmlm w-bqrm w-ʿnzm “camels, cattle and goats”.

evidence.locator: SEM000082 gml [camel] N, GEZ001984 gamal [camel] N

doctrine.statement: גְּמוּל is both what a man deals out and what comes back to him: “as you have done, it shall be done to you; your dealing shall return on your own head” (Oba 1:15); “the dealing of his hands shall be done to him” (Isa 3:11); “return to them their dealing … according to the work of their hands” (Psa 28:4; Lam 3:64). Yahweh is “a God of recompenses” who will surely repay (Jer 51:56), and the call “flee from the midst of Babylon … it is the time of Yahweh’s vengeance; he is repaying her a recompense” (Jer 51:6), with “happy he who repays you your dealing which you dealt to us” (Psa 137:8), is taken up for the Babylon of Revelation: “come out of her, my people … repay her as she repaid, and double to her double according to her works” (Rev 18:4–6). The same holds for good: he who is gracious to the poor lends to Yahweh, “and his dealing he will repay to him” (Pro 19:17), which the Lord carries to “you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just” (Luk 14:14). From the verses: a man’s deeds are not lost but return to him from God, at the day of judgment and the resurrection; as Paul says, “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Gal 6:7).

Yahweh’s dealing is not only requital. “He has not done to us according to our sins, nor dealt with us according to our iniquities” (Psa 103:10), and the psalm that says so begins “forget not all his dealings”: he forgives, heals and redeems (Psa 103:2–4). Isaiah remembers “all that Yahweh has dealt to us … according to his compassions and the greatness of his kindnesses” (Isa 63:7), and the psalmists sing that he “has dealt bountifully with me” (Psa 13:6; 116:7). The answer asked of the one so dealt with is a return: “What shall I return to Yahweh for all his benefits to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of Yahweh” (Psa 116:12–13); Hezekiah’s failure was that he “did not return according to the dealing done to him, for his heart was lifted up” (2Ch 32:25), and Israel is rebuked, “Do you deal thus with Yahweh … is he not your father?” (Deu 32:6). From the verses: God deals with his people better than their sins deserve, and that dealing lays on them a debt of thanks and faithfulness, not of payment.

note: Root key גמל as the database keys it. Proper names left to their own entries: גַּמְלִיאֵל (names/gamaliel.json, c.cj.af); גָּמוּל, the Levite of 1Ch 24:17 (c.cj.ac), and גְּמַלִּי, the Danite of Num 13:12 (c.cj.ah), have no name entries yet; בֵּית גָּמוּל (Jer 48:23) is a place, and the brief files its one token under the verb (c.cj.aa) as well. The verb’s three uses (deal out; wean; ripen) are kept together: no cognate yet found shares wean or ripen, and the proposed common sense “bring to full measure” rests on Arabic jamala “sum up” only. Akkadian gamālu is filed by the Proto-Semitic list under *gmr “spare”, so whether it belongs here or with Hebrew גמר “end, complete” should be checked in CAD. The camel’s tie to the root is unknown; Arabic keeps camel, beauty and collecting under one root too. Ge’ez ገመል is cited only from the Proto-Semitic list; Dillmann or Leslau should be consulted. Phoenician gml “camel” is a lead not yet found in Krahmalkov’s text. The Greek κάμηλος is recorded as a loan from the Semitic word; Abbott-Smith gives only the LXX equation, and Thayer, which derives it from גָּמָל (“Hebr. גָּמָל”), is cited for the derivation.
